results.title: Facebook AI and the Index Factory | Pinecone
results.content: In the world of vector search, there are many indexing methods and vector processing techniques that allow us to prioritize between recall, latency, and memory usage. For example, we can use an inverted file (IVF) index to reduce the scope of our search (increasing search speed), and then add a compression technique such as product quantization (PQ) to keep larger indexes within a reasonable size limit. In this article, we will learn how to build high-performance composite indexes using Facebook AI Similarity Search (Faiss) — a powerful library used by many for building fast and accurate vector similarity search indexes. Let’s put together a composite index where we pre-process vectors with OPQ, cluster with IVF, quantize using PQ, then re-order with a flat index. d = xb.shape[1] # in index string, m==32, nlist==256, nbits is 8 by default index = faiss.index_factory(d, "OPQ32,IVF256,PQ32,RFlat") # train and index vectors index.train(xb) index.add(xb). The search is referred to as being *asymmetric* because it compares `xq` — which is not compressed, against compressed PQ vectors (that we previously indexed). index = faiss.index_factory(d, "IVF256,PQ32x8") index.train(xb) index.add(xb) D, I = index.search(xq, k) recall(I). With this, we create an IVFADC index with `256` IVF cells; each vector is compressed with PQ using `m` and `nbits` values of `32` and `8`, respectively. # we can add pre-processing vector rotation to # improve distribution for the PQ step using OPQ index = faiss.index_factory(d, "OPQ32,IVF256,PQ32x8") index.train(xb) index.add(xb) D, I = index.search(xq, k) recall(I). ivf = faiss.extract_index_ivf(index) ivf.nprobe = 13 D, I = index.search(xq, k) recall(I). imi = faiss.extract_index_ivf(index) # access nprobe imi.nprobe = 620 D, I = index.search(xq, k) recall(I). imi = faiss.extract_index_ivf(index) # we increase nprobe imi.nprobe = 100 D, I = index.search(xq, k) recall(I). For a recall of 74%, our OPQ multi-D-ADC index is fastest at an average search time of just 461µs. Compared to our previous two indexes, IVF with HNSW produces comparable or better speed and significantly higher recall — at the cost of *much* higher memory usage. D, I = index.search(xq, k) recall(I). If a lower recall is acceptable for minimizing search time and memory usage, the IVF+HNSW index with OPQ is ideal.

results.title: Vector Database Basics: HNSW, IVF, PQ—Index Types & Best Practices - DevBlogIt 2025
results.content: This beginner-friendly guide explains the core ideas in plain English, shows how embeddings and ANN indexes (like HNSW/IVF-PQ) power semantic search, and when to use vectors vs. At its core, a vector database does three things very well: **turn items into embeddings, index those embeddings for fast lookup, and retrieve the nearest neighbors** for any new query. nlist = 4096 quantizer = faiss.IndexFlatIP(384) # coarse quantizer index = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(quantizer, 384, nlist, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT) index.train(embeddings) # learns centroids index.add(embeddings) # assigns vectors to lists index.nprobe = 32 # how many lists to scan per query. With embeddings created, indexed, and searchable—with filters and durability—you’ve got the full mental model of what a vector database actually does in production.## 4) Common use cases: Vector databases show up wherever meaning matters more than exact words. Keyword search excels at exact terms and Boolean filters; relational databases excel at transactions and structured queries; vector databases excel at meaning. # pip install sentence-transformers faiss-cpu from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer import faiss import numpy as np # 1) Embed a small corpus model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2") docs = [ "How to fix a leaky faucet", "Beginner's guide to replacing a tap washer", "Top 10 Italian pasta recipes", "Troubleshooting a dripping sink" ] X = model.encode(docs, normalize_embeddings=True).astype("float32") # 2) Build a FAISS index (cosine via inner product with normalized vectors) d = X.shape[1] index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d) index.add(X) # 3) Query query = "repair dripping tap" qvec = model.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True).astype("float32") D, I = index.search(qvec, k=3) for rank, idx in enumerate(I[0], 1): print(rank, docs[idx], D[0][rank-1]). -- In Postgres (with the pgvector extension installed) CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector; CREATE TABLE articles ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, body TEXT, tags TEXT[], embedding vector(768) ); -- Insert (embedding values come from your app) INSERT INTO articles (title, body, tags, embedding) VALUES ( 'Fixing a leaky faucet', 'Step-by-step guide to stop a dripping sink...', ARRAY['plumbing','how-to'], '[0.012, -0.034, ...]'::vector ); -- Similarity search (cosine distance) SELECT id, title FROM articles ORDER BY embedding <#> '[0.001, 0.045, ...]'::vector LIMIT 5; -- Filter + vector search (hybrid) SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE 'how-to' = ANY(tags) ORDER BY embedding <#> '[0.001, 0.045, ...]'::vector LIMIT 5;.

results.title: Product quantization PQ indexing method - Rohan's Bytes
results.content: *Product Quantization (PQ)* is a common compression-based indexing technique that addresses this by storing vectors in a compact coded form (4bit-Quantization in Vector-Embedding for RAG). In essence, PQ trades off a small amount of accuracy for major gains in memory footprint and search speed, making it attractive for large-scale LLM document retrieval (Accelerating Vector Search: NVIDIA cuVS IVF-PQ Part 1, Deep Dive | NVIDIA Technical Blog). In the following, we review how PQ indexing works and its trade-offs, recent PQ variant advancements (OPQ, residual PQ, and 2024–2025 innovations), and compare PQ-based indexes with other popular vector search methods like HNSW and IVF in the context of LLM retrieval. In summary, PQ indexing’s main appeal is **memory efficiency** (storing compact codes instead of full vectors) and improved search speed on large datasets, at the expense of some retrieval accuracy and added index training complexity (Accelerating Vector Search: NVIDIA cuVS IVF-PQ Part 1, Deep Dive | NVIDIA Technical Blog). For example, a recent study characterized the trade-offs: an IVF-PQ index (with 16,384 clusters and 8-bit PQ) used **7.2× less memory** than an HNSW index (with scalar-quantized vectors) for a 100M corpus, but reached only ~70% of HNSW’s recall . One approach is to use HNSW on top of PQ codes – e.g. build the HNSW graph over compressed vectors to reduce memory. The key is understanding the trade-offs: PQ indexing offers compactness, HNSW offers accuracy, and IVF offers scalability, and modern systems often mix and match these to meet the needs of large-scale LLM retrieval. An HNSW index (with 8-bit quantized vectors) attained ~**87%** recall but used large memory, whereas an IVF-PQ index (16k clusters, 256-byte PQ codes) used about **7.2× less memory** yet maxed out around **61%** recall (Towards Understanding Systems Trade-offs in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Model Inference). NVIDIA’s IVF-PQ index for the DEEP1B dataset compressed **1 billion, 96-D vectors from 360 GiB to ~54 GiB** – a **6–7×** compression – *with negligible impact on search accuracy* (verified at >0.95 recall) (Accelerating Vector Search: NVIDIA cuVS IVF-PQ Part 1, Deep Dive | NVIDIA Technical Blog).

results.title: Blog 2: Vector Quantization, IVF, and Beyond – Laying the Groundwork for Large-Scale ANN Systems | by Jatin Bhateja | Medium
results.content: Blog 2: Vector Quantization, IVF, and Beyond – Laying the Groundwork for Large-Scale ANN Systems. Following our deep dive into HNSW, it’s time to switch gears and explore another powerful family of ANN algorithms: vector quantization-based techniques. These methods offer a memory-efficient and scalable way to handle billion-scale vector datasets. This blog focuses on Inverted File Index (IVF) and sets the stage for Product Quantization (PQ), a widely-used compression method. Together, they form the foundation of real-world vector search systems like FAISS. Part 1: The Motivation for IVF and PQ. Even with graph-based methods like HNSW, memory becomes a bottleneck when handling billions of vectors. Vector quantization offers a trade-off:. Fast search via indexing and compression. Assign each vector to the closest centroid. Starts with a random vector. Part 3: The IVF Index Structure. Once vectors are clustered, we construct an inverted index, much like in text search engines. 1. Run k-means to compute centroids. 2. Assign each data vector to its nearest centroid. 3. Store the vector in the list (or "inverted list") associated with that centroid. This way, instead of storing all vectors in one place, we split the dataset into K buckets, each tied to a centroid. 1. Compute L2 distance between query vector and all centroids. 4. Collect top-k closest vectors overall. Part 4: IVF Search Walkthrough. Dataset size = 1 million vectors. 2. Traverse vectors under those centroids (say ~10K vectors). Use hierarchical k-means or HNSW over centroids. Store vector codes instead of full vectors. Product Quantization divides vectors into sub-vectors and quantizes them independently. Divide a d-dimensional vector into m parts. Store the code index (not the vector itself). Part 7: Combining IVF with PQ. IVF narrows the search scope. 1. Use IVF to find candidate lists. FAISS: Meta's open-source ANN library; supports IVF, PQ, HNSW, and hybrids. Part 9: Comparing IVF+PQ vs HNSW. Latency Low (w/ PQ) Very Low. ANN search isn’t about picking one algorithm. For extreme scale and memory constraints: IVF+PQ. For hybrid needs: Combine them (e.g., HNSW over PQ centroids). Now that we understand IVF and PQ, we’ll go deeper into Product Quantization internals, covering encoding, decoding, distance computation, and more.
